## Initial assignment (`--init`)

Restart 0 starts from one of four starts (later restarts are always random):

- `--init majority` (default): every variable takes its majority polarity.
- `--init rarest`: deterministic constructive start (no RNG), rarest variables first.
- `--init glowest`: deterministic constructive start, most frequent variables first.
- `--init likho`: all false, then a neutral/switch-domain repair pass.
- `-deep-dive VARS NODES`: implies `--init likho`, caps switch domains at VARS
  variables, gives each prime at most NODES search nodes, and fires domains
  before neutral repairs.
- `-pre-cook zero|majority|rarest|glowest`: implies `--init likho`; phase 1 is
  that assignment instead of the default all-false one (a partially solved input).

The four starts work in both `plain` and `groups` mode; `-deep-dive` is a variant
of `likho`.

### Rarest / Glowest

`rarest` and `glowest` are the same constructive start with the selection order
reversed:

1. Repeatedly set an unassigned variable: `rarest` takes the **fewest** clauses
   holding `x` or `!x`, whichever count is larger, `glowest` the **most**, and only
   clauses that are not yet satisfied count (ties by id). The counts are recomputed
   after every assignment, so satisfying a clause removes that overlap from every
   variable still unset.
2. The variable takes the value that satisfies more **forced**
   clauses (open clauses where it is the last unset variable); else more **open**
   (not yet satisfied) clauses; else the larger total polarity; else `false`.

### Likho

`--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
`false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no
satisfied clause, and each variable is flipped at most once:

- A **neutral** variable inside a rogue clause is flipped immediately; it breaks
  nothing and satisfies at least that clause.
- A **prime** is the sole support of some satisfied clause, so flipping it alone
  breaks that clause. Its **switch domain** is the set of other unflipped variables
  that must flip with it so every clause it breaks gains a new true literal. A
  repair may itself be a prime, so a domain chains: prime -> prime -> ... -> neutral.
  The domain is accepted only if the joint flip leaves every touched clause
  satisfied. A twin pair is the special case of a domain with one partner.
- Domains are recomputed after every firing, and the gold rule (every variable
  fires once) means two primes whose domains share a variable share that single
  flip, while a prime whose domain conflicts with an already fired one is simply
  not fired.
- A neutral flip can liberate a prime (the clause it was propping up gets another
  true literal); the next pass sees it as neutral and can flip it. By default
  domains are tried only when no neutral is left anywhere; `-deep-dive` reverses
  that order and tries a closed domain first.

A domain is capped at 8 variables and its closure search at 64 backtracking nodes,
so a prime with an unusually large or conflicting domain is skipped rather than
solved. `-deep-dive VARS NODES` raises or lowers both bounds. With the default
zero start the repair is deterministic for a given formula; `-pre-cook majority`
inherits the majority phase's RNG tie-breaking.

```
### Min-overlapping

`min-overlapping` reuses the same value rule but ranks by how much a variable
overlaps the part of the formula already solved:

1. The first variable is `glowest`'s pick (most clauses holding `x` or `!x`,
   whichever count is larger, ties by id).
2. After that, each step takes the unset variable with the smallest
   **(occurrences in satisfied clauses) / (total occurrences)**, ties by id; a
   variable that occurs nowhere has no ratio and goes last.
3. The value rule is the same forced > open > total polarity > false.

The idea is to keep the next variable mostly outside the clauses the first pick
already satisfied, so the remaining search is not dragged into the same
subsystem. It starts worse than `glowest` (more broken clauses) but the search
finishes faster on 3-SAT: at 1000/3.5 it needs 7.2k flips vs glowest's 19.4k.
```

`glowest` is the best init here. It leaves fewer broken clauses than rarest-new on
every random row (4.5 vs 28, 37 vs 98, 274 vs 631, 783 vs 2024) and at 20000/3.5 it
is the only start that solves all 10 seeds (init 783, 129k flips, 0.9 s vs 2.4 s for
majority). On the AIM yes-set it has the lowest init count (16.7) and solves the same
31 instances as rarest. Taking the highest-overlap variables first pays off where
rarest's low-overlap-first pass leaves clauses hanging on a single literal.

The zero start still leaves 3-5x fewer broken clauses than majority, and it solves
1000/2.0 outright at init (zero flips), but it is a much deeper local minimum. At
20000/3.5 it solves **0/10** at this budget, where majority and both rarest orders
solve 9/10 (glowest 10/10); fewer broken clauses does not mean an easier search.
`-pre-cook majority` restores the previous majority-start repair exactly (209
broken, 9/10, 129k flips), so pre-cooking is the escape from the zero-start basin.
On the AIM yes-set the zero start matches both rarest orders at 31/48 (majority and
the majority pre-cook stay at 27/48), so the constructive start pays off there.
`-deep-dive 32 128` trims the zero-start init count (637 at 20000, 337 at 5000) but
changes no solved count. From a majority pre-cook, domains-first makes 20000/3.5
much worse (1/10 at 32 128, 0/3 at the default bounds), so deep-dive is not the
escape route; pre-cook without it is. `majority` stays the default start for the
plain search.

The max-of-polarities rarest order leaves 2-3x fewer broken clauses than majority,
but ~30% more than the total-occurrence order. It is faster on 1000-var/3.5 and
20000-var/3.5, slower on 5000-var/3.9; on the AIM yes-set both rarest orders solve
the same 31/48 (identical failure sets) versus 27/48 for majority. It changes which
near-solutions are reachable more than it changes total coverage.

Rarest-first is still **worse** than majority at scale. Why: it satisfies each clause
with the first literal it can and never adds redundancy, so almost
every satisfied clause hangs on a single variable. On the 20000-var / ratio 3.5 instance
77% of variables are prime after rarest-first (62% after majority), only 23% are neutral
(38%), and 63% of the broken clauses contain no neutral variable at all, i.e. no free flip
(26% after majority) -- measured with the old ordering. Fewer problems, but most of the
remaining ones cannot be fixed
without breaking something. Likho attacks exactly that: a prime's switch domain
chains through other primes until it reaches a neutral, instead of giving up at the
first broken clause. Group mode's merge, which only fires neutrals,
is hit the same way: its leftover barely changed (e.g. 105.7 -> 95.0 unmerged at ratio
4.2).

### Rarest / Glowest / Min-overlapping

All three use the same value rule: the picked variable takes the value that
satisfies more **forced** clauses (open clauses where it is the last unset
variable); else more **open** (not yet satisfied) clauses; else the larger total
polarity; else `false`.

They differ only in which unset variable is picked next:

- `rarest` takes the **fewest** clauses holding `x` or `!x`, whichever count is
  larger; `glowest` the **most**. Only clauses that are not yet satisfied count
  (ties by id), recomputed after every assignment, so satisfying a clause removes
  that overlap from every variable still unset.
- `min-overlapping` takes `glowest`'s pick first, then at every step the unset
  variable with the smallest **(occurrences in satisfied clauses) / (total
  occurrences)** (ties by id). A variable that occurs nowhere has no ratio and
  goes last. The point is to keep picking variables mostly outside the clauses
  the first pick already satisfied, instead of following the same subsystem.

### Likho

`--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
`false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no
satisfied clause, and each variable is flipped at most once:

- A **neutral** variable inside a rogue clause is flipped immediately; it breaks
  nothing and satisfies at least that clause.

    }
    free(unset); free(done); free(pos); free(neg); free(overlap); free(total);
    free(assigned); free(heap);
    rebuild_counts(s);
    return true;
}

bool solver_init_glowest(Solver *s) { return init_order(s, ORDER_GLOWEST); }

```c
/* ---- Gob: linear relaxation of the clause system ------------------------ */

/* Each clause becomes the signed linear equation sum(+-x) = 1 (a positive
 * literal is +x, a negative one -x). Cyclic Kaczmarz projections solve it in
 * the least-squares sense, the vector is shifted so no value is negative, and
 * round(v + shift) mod 2 decodes it to booleans. The shift is scanned over a
 * few fractional offsets and the decode with the fewest unsatisfied clauses
 * wins (ties: smallest shift). Deterministic, no RNG. */
#define GOB_SWEEPS 64
#define GOB_SHIFTS 16   /* base shift + k/4, k = 0..15 */

bool solver_init_gob(Solver *s) {
    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);
    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);
    bool *best = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *best);
    if (!v || !a || !best) { free(v); free(a); free(best); return false; }
    for (size_t sweep = 0; sweep < GOB_SWEEPS; sweep++) {
        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++) {
            const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
            size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
            if (len == 0) continue;
            double sum = 0;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
            double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
        }
    }
    double lo = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) if (v[i] < lo) lo = v[i];
    long long base = (long long)(-lo);          /* ceil: v + base >= 0 */
    if ((double)base < -lo) base++;
    size_t best_unsat = SIZE_MAX;
    for (int k = 0; k < GOB_SHIFTS; k++) {
        double shift = (double)base + (double)k / 4.0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
            long long t = (long long)(v[i] + shift + 0.5);
            a[i] = (t & 1) != 0;
        }
        solver_set_assignment(s, a);
        size_t u = solver_unsatisfied_count(s);
        if (u < best_unsat) { best_unsat = u; memcpy(best, a, nv * sizeof *best); }
    }
    solver_set_assignment(s, best);
    free(v); free(a); free(best);
    return true;
}
```

`lo` starts at 0 so base = ceil(-min(0, min v)) ≥ 0; if all v ≥ 0, base=0. Since v starts at 0 and may be updated negatively. Using lo=0 means we include unused vars (v=0) → base ≥ 0 always. The spec says eliminate negatives, so base = max(0, ceil(-min)). ✓

The ceil computation: `-lo` is ≥ 0. `base = (long long)(-lo)` truncates toward zero; if `(double)base < -lo`, increment. ✓ (e.g., -lo=1.7 → base=1, 1<1.7 → 2).

```json
  "oldString": "/* ---- Gob: linear relaxation of the clause system ------------------------ */\n\n/* Every clause becomes the signed equation sum(+-x) = 1: a positive literal is\n * +x, a negative one -x. Cyclic Kaczmarz projections (one per clause per sweep)\n * solve it in the least-squares sense; the vector is then shifted so no value is\n * negative and round(v + shift) mod 2 decodes it to booleans. Only the shift is\n * free, so a few fractional offsets are scanned and the decode with the fewest\n * unsatisfied clauses wins (ties: smallest shift). Deterministic, no RNG. */\n#define GOB_SWEEPS 64     /* Kaczmarz passes over the whole clause system */\n#define GOB_SHIFTS 16     /* decode candidates: base shift + k/4 */\n\nbool solver_init_gob(Solver *s) {\n    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;\n    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;\n    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);\n    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);\n    bool *best = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *best);\n    if (!v || !a || !best) { free(v); free(a); free(best); return false; }\n    for (size_t sweep = 0; sweep < GOB_SWEEPS; sweep++) {\n        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++) {\n            const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);\n            size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);\n            if (len == 0) continue;\n            double sum = 0;\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)\n                sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];\n            double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)\n                v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;\n        }\n    }\n    double lo = 0;                                   /* shift so v + base >= 0 */\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) if (v[i] < lo) lo = v[i];\n    long long base = (long long)(-lo);\n    if ((double)base < -lo) base++;\n    size_t best_unsat = SIZE_MAX;\n    for (int k = 0; k < GOB_SHIFTS; k++) {\n        double shift = (double)base + (double)k / 4.0;\n        for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {\n            long long t = (long long)(v[i] + shift + 0.5);   /* round to nearest */\n            a[i] = (t & 1) != 0;\n        }\n        solver_set_assignment(s, a);\n        size_t u = solver_unsatisfied_count(s);\n        if (u < best_unsat) { best_unsat = u; memcpy(best, a, nv * sizeof *best); }\n    }\n    solver_set_assignment(s, best);\n    free(v); free(a); free(best);\n    return true;\n}",
  "path": "/home/evg/i_C_u/little.AI/knowledge/c_3sat/src/sat.c"
}
```

```c
static void test_init_gob_hand_checked(void) {
    /* Units pin the decode: the clause 1 is +x = 1, -2 is -x = 1 (shifted to
     * false), 3 is +x = 1. So the start is exactly (true, false, true). */
    Cnf c = must_parse("p cnf 3 3\n1 0\n-2 0\n3 0\n");
    Solver *s = must_solver(&c, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    const bool *a = solver_assignment(s);
    CHECK(a[0] && !a[1] && a[2]);
    CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&c);

    /* A single clause 1 2 projects to (1/2, 1/2): both round up and satisfy it. */
    Cnf d = must_parse("p cnf 2 1\n1 2 0\n");
    s = must_solver(&d, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    a = solver_assignment(s);
    CHECK(a[0] && a[1] && solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&d);

    /* Mixed signs: (1 -2) projects to (1/2, -1/2); -1/2 shifts to +1/2, so both
     * decode true and the clause holds. */
    Cnf e = must_parse("p cnf 2 1\n1 -2 0\n");
    s = must_solver(&e, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    a = solver_assignment(s);
    CHECK(a[0] && a[1] && solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&e);

    /* Empty clause and empty formula: no crash, the empty clause stays rogue. */
    Cnf f = must_parse("p cnf 1 1\n0\n");
    s = must_solver(&f, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 1);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&f);

    Cnf g = must_parse("p cnf 0 0\n");
    s = must_solver(&g, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&g);
}
```

/* Benchmark of the starts -- majority, old/new rarest, glowest, min-overlapping,
 * Gob, Likho, Likho deep-dive, Likho pre-cooked with majority -- on random 3-SAT
 * or a DIMACS file.
 *
 * The previous total-occurrence rarest order is reimplemented here as a
 * baseline (O(nv * clauses), benchmark-sized inputs only) and injected through
 * SolverConfig.initial, so all starts run the same search code.
 *
 * usage:
 *   bench_rarest <n> <ratio> <seeds> <steps> <restarts>
 *   bench_rarest <file.cnf> <steps> <restarts>
 *
 * steps = 0 measures only the init quality (no search).
 * Every SAT result is verified against the formula before it is counted.
 */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <time.h>
#include "sat.h"

/* ---- random 3-SAT ------------------------------------------------------ */

typedef struct { uint64_t s; } R;
static uint64_t nx(R *r) { uint64_t x = r->s; x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17; return r->s = x; }
static size_t idx(R *r, size_t n) { return (size_t)(nx(r) % n); }

typedef struct { size_t nv, nc, *off; int *lits; } Gen;

static void gen_free(Gen *g) { free(g->off); free(g->lits); }

/* Three distinct variables per clause, random polarity. */
static Gen gen3(size_t nv, size_t nc, uint64_t seed) {
    Gen g = { nv, nc, malloc((nc + 1) * sizeof *g.off), malloc(nc * 3 * sizeof *g.lits) };
    R r = { seed ? seed : 1 };
    g.off[0] = 0;
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++) {
        size_t a = idx(&r, nv), b = idx(&r, nv - 1), d = idx(&r, nv - 2);
        if (b >= a) b++;
        if (d >= a) d++;
        if (d >= b) d++;
        int s[3];
        for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) s[k] = (nx(&r) & 1) ? 1 : -1;
        g.lits[3*c+0] = s[0] * (int)(a + 1);
        g.lits[3*c+1] = s[1] * (int)(b + 1);
        g.lits[3*c+2] = s[2] * (int)(d + 1);
        g.off[c+1] = g.off[c] + 3;
    }
    return g;
}

static char *to_dimacs(const Gen *g) {
    size_t cap = g->nc * 32 + 64;
    char *s = malloc(cap), *p = s;
    p += sprintf(p, "p cnf %zu %zu\n", g->nv, g->nc);
    for (size_t c = 0; c < g->nc; c++) {
        for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) p += sprintf(p, "%d ", g->lits[3*c+k]);
        *p++ = '0'; *p++ = '\n'; *p = '\0';
    }

/* ---- old rarest: static order by total occurrences, ties by id --------- */

static void old_rarest(const Cnf *cnf, bool *a) {
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    size_t *cnt = calloc(nv, sizeof *cnt), *order = malloc(nv * sizeof *order);
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++)
        for (size_t k = 0; k < cnf_clause_len(cnf, c); k++) cnt[cnf_clause(cnf, c)[k].var]++;
    for (size_t v = 0; v < nv; v++) order[v] = v;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++)
        for (size_t j = i + 1; j < nv; j++)
            if (cnt[order[j]] < cnt[order[i]]) { size_t t = order[i]; order[i] = order[j]; order[j] = t; }
    uint32_t *unset = malloc(nc * sizeof *unset);
    unsigned char *done = calloc(nc, 1);
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++) unset[c] = (uint32_t)cnf_clause_len(cnf, c);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        size_t v = order[i], fp = 0, fn = 0, op = 0, on = 0, tp = 0, tn = 0;
        for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++)
            for (size_t k = 0; k < cnf_clause_len(cnf, c); k++) {
                const Lit l = cnf_clause(cnf, c)[k];
                if (l.var != v) continue;
                if (l.positive) tp++; else tn++;
                if (done[c]) continue;
                if (unset[c] == 1) { if (l.positive) fp++; else fn++; }
                else { if (l.positive) op++; else on++; }
            }
        bool val = (fp != fn) ? fp > fn : (op != on) ? op > on : (tp != tn) ? tp > tn : false;
        a[v] = val;
        for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++)
            for (size_t k = 0; k < cnf_clause_len(cnf, c); k++) {
                const Lit l = cnf_clause(cnf, c)[k];
                if (l.var != v) continue;
                unset[c]--;
                if (!done[c] && l.positive == val) done[c] = 1;
            }
    }
    free(cnt); free(order); free(unset); free(done);
}

85: 
86: ## Initial assignment (`--init`)
87: 
88: Restart 0 starts from one of five starts (later restarts are always random):
89: 
90: - `--init majority` (default): every variable takes its majority polarity.
91: - `--init rarest`: deterministic constructive start (no RNG), rarest variables first.
92: - `--init glowest`: deterministic constructive start, most frequent variables first.
93: - `--init min-overlapping`: deterministic constructive start, first the most
94:   frequent variable, then the one overlapping the solved part least.
95: - `--init likho`: all false, then a neutral/switch-domain repair pass.
96: - `-deep-dive VARS NODES`: implies `--init likho`, caps switch domains at VARS
97:   variables, gives each prime at most NODES search nodes, and fires domains
98:   before neutral repairs.
99: - `-pre-cook zero|majority|rarest|glowest|min-overlapping`: implies `--init likho`;
100:   phase 1 is that assignment instead of the default all-false one (a partially
101:   solved input).
102: 
103: The five starts work in both `plain` and `groups` mode; `-deep-dive` is a variant
104: of `likho`.
105: 
106: ### Rarest / Glowest / Min-overlapping
107: 
108: All three use the same value rule: the picked variable takes the value that
109: satisfies more **forced** clauses (open clauses where it is the last unset
110: variable); else more **open** (not yet satisfied) clauses; else the larger total
111: polarity; else `false`.
112: 
113: They differ only in which unset variable is picked next:
114: 
115: - `rarest` takes the **fewest** clauses holding `x` or `!x`, whichever count is
116:   larger; `glowest` the **most**. Only clauses that are not yet satisfied count
117:   (ties by id), recomputed after every assignment, so satisfying a clause removes
118:   that overlap from every variable still unset.
119: - `min-overlapping` takes `glowest`'s pick first, then at every step the unset
120:   variable with the smallest **(occurrences in satisfied clauses) / (total
121:   occurrences)** (ties by id). A variable that occurs nowhere has no ratio and
122:   goes last. The point is to keep picking variables mostly outside the clauses
123:   the first pick already satisfied, instead of following the same subsystem.
124: 
125: ### Likho
126: 
127: `--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
128: `false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no
129: satisfied clause, and each variable is flipped at most once:
130: 
131: - A **neutral** variable inside a rogue clause is flipped immediately; it breaks
132:   nothing and satisfies at least that clause.
133: - A **prime** is the sole support of some satisfied clause, so flipping it alone
134:   breaks that clause. Its **switch domain** is the set of other unflipped variables
135:   that must flip with it so every clause it breaks gains a new true literal. A
136:   repair may itself be a prime, so a domain chains: prime -> prime -> ... -> neutral.
137:   The domain is accepted only if the joint flip leaves every touched clause
138:   satisfied. A twin pair is the special case of a domain with one partner.
139: - Domains are recomputed after every firing, and the gold rule (every variable
140:   fires once) means two primes whose domains share a variable share that single
141:   flip, while a prime whose domain conflicts with an already fired one is simply
142:   not fired.
143: - A neutral flip can liberate a prime (the clause it was propping up gets another
144:   true literal); the next pass sees it as neutral and can flip it. By default
145:   domains are tried only when no neutral is left anywhere; `-deep-dive` reverses
146:   that order and tries a closed domain first.
147: 
148: A domain is capped at 8 variables and its closure search at 64 backtracking nodes,
149: so a prime with an unusually large or conflicting domain is skipped rather than
150: solved. `-deep-dive VARS NODES` raises or lowers both bounds. With the default
151: zero start the repair is deterministic for a given formula; `-pre-cook majority`
152: inherits the majority phase's RNG tie-breaking.
153: 
154: ### Measurements
155: 
156: Measured on random 3-SAT, 10 seeds per row (3 seeds for the 5000-var row), 20
157: restarts, default solver seed. "old" is the previous total-occurrence rarest order,
158: kept for comparison; "likho-dd" is `-deep-dive 32 128`, "likho-pc" is
159: `-pre-cook majority`. All eight starts share the same search code:
160: 
161: | instance | broken after init (maj / old / new / glow / mo / likho / dd / pc) | solved | mean flips over solved (maj / old / new / glow / mo / likho / dd / pc) |
162: |---|---|---|---|
163: | 1000 vars, ratio 2.0 | 78 / 15 / 28 / 4.5 / 12.7 / 0 / 0.2 / 0 | 10/10 each | 88 / 47 / 67 / 26 / 27 / 0 / 1 / 0 |
164: | 1000 vars, ratio 3.5 | 187 / 77 / 98 / 37 / 58 / 34 / 32 / 10 | 10/10 each | 11.1k / 16.1k / 12.0k / 19.4k / 7.2k / 18.1k / 17.6k / 9.8k |
165: | 20000 vars, ratio 3.5 | 3802 / 1527 / 2024 / 783 / 1213 / 742 / 637 / 209 | 9/10, 9/10, 9/10, 10/10, 8/10, 0/10, 0/10, 9/10 | 123k / 169k / 162k / 129k / 143k / — / — / 129k |
166: | 5000 vars, ratio 3.9 | 1098 / 482 / 631 / 274 / 396 / 385 / 337 / 126 | 2/3 each | 3.06M / 0.76M / 1.84M / 4.40M / 4.40M / 4.40M / 4.40M / 5.68M |
167: | AIM yes-set, 48 instances | 46 / 18 / 21 / 16.7 / 19.0 / 23 / 22 / 22 | 27 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 27 | — |

173: 31 instances as rarest. Taking the highest-overlap variables first pays off where

194: escape route; pre-cook without it is. `majority` stays the default start for the
195: plain search.
196: 
197: The max-of-polarities rarest order leaves 2-3x fewer broken clauses than majority,
198: but ~30% more than the total-occurrence order. It is faster on 1000-var/3.5 and
199: 20000-var/3.5, slower on 5000-var/3.9; on the AIM yes-set both rarest orders solve
200: the same 31/48 (identical failure sets) versus 27/48 for majority. It changes which
201: near-solutions are reachable more than it changes total coverage.

```
### Gob

`--init gob` is a linear relaxation, not a clause walk. Each clause becomes the
signed equation `sum(±x) = 1` (a positive literal is `+x`, a negative one `-x`),
and 64 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps project the all-zero vector onto the system
(one exact projection per clause per sweep). Each value is then shifted by the
smallest non-negative amount (`ceil(-v)`), rounded to the nearest integer and
taken mod 2, which decodes the real vector to booleans. A shift is applied per
variable rather than globally because a global one cannot satisfy mixed-sign
units: `(x)` and `(-x)` always decode to the same parity.

The decode is only a starting point, so four greedy passes follow: a variable
whose bit satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks is flipped, using the
same incremental counts as the search. Deterministic, no RNG.
```

```json
  "newString": "Restart 0 starts from one of six starts (later restarts are always random):\n\n- `--init majority` (default): every variable takes its majority polarity.\n- `--init rarest`: deterministic constructive start (no RNG), rarest variables first.\n- `--init glowest`: deterministic constructive start, most frequent variables first.\n- `--init min-overlapping`: deterministic constructive start, first the most\n  frequent variable, then the one overlapping the solved part least.\n- `--init gob`: deterministic linear-relaxation start (no RNG), clauses as signed\n  equations solved by Kaczmarz sweeps and decoded mod 2.\n- `--init likho`: all false, then a neutral/switch-domain repair pass.\n- `-deep-dive VARS NODES`: implies `--init likho`, caps switch domains at VARS\n  variables, gives each prime at most NODES search nodes, and fires domains\n  before neutral repairs.\n- `-pre-cook zero|majority|rarest|glowest|min-overlapping|gob`: implies `--init likho`;\n  phase 1 is that assignment instead of the default all-false one (a partially\n  solved input).\n\nThe six starts work in both `plain` and `groups` mode; `-deep-dive` is a variant\nof `likho`.",
```

```json
{
  "newString": "### Gob\n\n`--init gob` is a linear relaxation, not a clause walk. Each clause becomes the\nsigned equation `sum(±x) = 1` (a positive literal is `+x`, a negative one `-x`),\nand 64 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps project the all-zero vector onto that system (one\nexact projection per clause per sweep). Each value is then shifted by the\nsmallest non-negative amount, rounded to the nearest integer and taken mod 2,\nwhich decodes the real vector to booleans. The shift is per variable, not global,\nbecause a global shift cannot satisfy mixed-sign units: `(x)` and `(-x)` always\ndecode to the same parity.\n\nThe decode is only a starting point, so four greedy passes follow: a variable\nwhose bit satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks is flipped, using the same\nincremental counts as the search. Deterministic, no RNG.\n\n### Likho",

  "path": "/home/evg/i_C_u/little.AI/knowledge/c_3sat/README.md"
```

127: ### Gob
128: 
129: `--init gob` is a linear relaxation, not a clause walk. Each clause becomes the
130: signed equation `sum(±x) = 1` (a positive literal is `+x`, a negative one `-x`),
131: and 64 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps project the all-zero vector onto that system (one
132: exact projection per clause per sweep). Each value is then shifted by the
133: smallest non-negative amount, rounded to the nearest integer and taken mod 2,
134: which decodes the real vector to booleans. The shift is per variable, not global,
135: because a global shift cannot satisfy mixed-sign units: `(x)` and `(-x)` always
136: decode to the same parity.
137: 
138: The decode is only a starting point, so four greedy passes follow: a variable
139: whose bit satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks is flipped, using the same
140: incremental counts as the search. Deterministic, no RNG.
141: 
142: ### Likho
143: 
144: `--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
145: `false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no
146: satisfied clause, and each variable is flipped at most once:
147: 
148: - A **neutral** variable inside a rogue clause is flipped immediately; it breaks
149:   nothing and satisfies at least that clause.
150: - A **prime** is the sole support of some satisfied clause, so flipping it alone
151:   breaks that clause. Its **switch domain** is the set of other unflipped variables
152:   that must flip with it so every clause it breaks gains a new true literal. A
153:   repair may itself be a prime, so a domain chains: prime -> prime -> ... -> neutral.
154:   The domain is accepted only if the joint flip leaves every touched clause
155:   satisfied. A twin pair is the special case of a domain with one partner.
156: - Domains are recomputed after every firing, and the gold rule (every variable
157:   fires once) means two primes whose domains share a variable share that single
158:   flip, while a prime whose domain conflicts with an already fired one is simply
159:   not fired.
160: - A neutral flip can liberate a prime (the clause it was propping up gets another
161:   true literal); the next pass sees it as neutral and can flip it. By default
162:   domains are tried only when no neutral is left anywhere; `-deep-dive` reverses
163:   that order and tries a closed domain first.
164: 
165: A domain is capped at 8 variables and its closure search at 64 backtracking nodes,
166: so a prime with an unusually large or conflicting domain is skipped rather than
167: solved. `-deep-dive VARS NODES` raises or lowers both bounds. With the default
168: zero start the repair is deterministic for a given formula; `-pre-cook majority`
169: inherits the majority phase's RNG tie-breaking.

/* Re-derive one variable's state, break and make counts from the current
 * assignment in a single pass over its occurrences.
 *
 * Ranking invariant (relied on by the group merge):
 *   VAR_PRIME   <=> break_count >= 1   (sole support of at least one solved clause)
 *   VAR_NEUTRAL <=> break_count == 0   (flipping can never un-solve a clause)
 * Neutrality is a property of the *current* assignment, not of the variable. */
static void refresh_var(Solver *s, size_t v) {
    size_t satisfied = 0, rogue_occ = 0, breaks = 0, min_support = SIZE_MAX;
    bool prime = false;
    bool val = s->assignment[v];
    for (size_t i = s->occ_off[v]; i < s->occ_off[v + 1]; i++) {
        Occ o = s->occ[i];
        uint32_t c = s->sat[o.clause];
        if (c == 0) { rogue_occ++; continue; }
        if (val == o.positive) {
            satisfied++;
            if (c < min_support) min_support = c;
            if (c == 1) { prime = true; breaks++; }
        }
    }
    VarStats *st = &s->stats[v];
    st->satisfied_occurrences = satisfied;
    st->rogue_occurrences = rogue_occ;
    st->break_count = breaks;
    st->make_count = rogue_occ;  /* a rogue clause has no true literal, so every incidence is a "make" */
    st->rank = SIZE_MAX;
    if (occ_count(s, v) == 0) { st->state = VAR_UNUSED; st->min_support = 0; }

/* ---- Gob: linear relaxation of the clause system ------------------------ */

/* Every clause becomes the signed equation sum(+-x) = 1: a positive literal is
 * +x, a negative one -x. Cyclic Kaczmarz projections (one per clause per sweep)
 * solve it in the least-squares sense. Each value is then shifted by the
 * smallest non-negative amount (so -x = 1 decodes to false, not true), rounded,
 * and taken mod 2. A greedy pass then flips a decoded variable whenever it
 * satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks, adapting the bits to the formula.
 * Deterministic, no RNG. */
#define GOB_SWEEPS 64     /* Kaczmarz passes over the whole clause system */
#define GOB_PASSES 4      /* greedy adaptation passes over the decoded bits */

bool solver_init_gob(Solver *s) {
    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);
    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);
    if (!v || !a) { free(v); free(a); return false; }
    for (size_t sweep = 0; sweep < GOB_SWEEPS; sweep++) {
        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++) {
            const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
            size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
            if (len == 0) continue;
            double sum = 0;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
            double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
        }
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        double u = v[i];
        if (u < 0) {                                  /* shift the negative away */
            long long sh = (long long)(-u);
            if ((double)sh < -u) sh++;
            u += (double)sh;
        }
        a[i] = (((long long)(u + 0.5)) & 1) != 0;     /* round to nearest, mod 2 */
    }
    solver_set_assignment(s, a);
    free(v); free(a);
    for (int pass = 0; pass < GOB_PASSES; pass++) {   /* step 4: best correlation */
        size_t flips = 0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
            refresh_var(s, i);
            const VarStats *st = &s->stats[i];
            if (st->make_count > st->break_count) { solver_flip(s, i); flips++; }
        }
        if (flips == 0) break;
    }
    return true;
}

Step 4 became a **greedy repair on the decoded booleans**, not a correlation with the real vector. Here's the whole thing (`src/sat.c`, end of `solver_init_gob`):

```c
for (int pass = 0; pass < GOB_PASSES; pass++) {   /* step 4: best correlation */
    size_t flips = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        refresh_var(s, i);
        const VarStats *st = &s->stats[i];
        if (st->make_count > st->break_count) { solver_flip(s, i); flips++; }
    }
    if (flips == 0) break;
}
```

**What the two numbers mean.** For variable `v` in the current assignment:

- `make_count` = number of *rogue* (unsatisfied) clauses containing `v` — each one gains a true literal if `v` flips.
- `break_count` = number of *satisfied* clauses where `v`'s literal is the **only** true one — each one goes rogue if `v` flips.

So one flip changes the unsatisfied total by exactly `break_count - make_count`. The condition `make > break` therefore means "this flip strictly reduces the number of broken clauses". Ties (`make == break`) do nothing, which avoids drift and keeps the pass deterministic.

**Other choices:**

- Variables are visited in id order, and `solver_flip` updates the counts incrementally, so later variables in the same pass already see earlier flips (Gauss–Seidel, not a frozen snapshot).
- Up to 4 passes (`GOB_PASSES`), stopping as soon as a pass flips nothing. Termination is actually guaranteed regardless of the cap: every accepted flip strictly lowers the unsat count, so the pass can only run out of improving moves.
- No RNG anywhere — same formula gives the same bits.

**What it is not.** The fractional Kaczmarz values are freed before this loop; step 4 never looks at them. It is a local one-variable-at-a-time hill climb on the true objective (satisfied clause count), not a global "maximize correlation between the real vector and ±1 booleans". A more literal reading of your step 4 could instead be: for each variable, pick the parity whose ±1 value has the larger dot product with the real `v_i` (e.g. flip when `v_i` sits closer to the other integer), possibly weighted by clause degree. That is a different heuristic and would need measuring; say the word if that's what you meant.

Skipped: no measurement of how much the greedy pass contributes on its own (it's folded into the reported init counts). Risk: with ties left unflipped, a chain that needs two simultaneous flips to pay off is invisible to this pass.

```c
            if (!len) continue;
            double sum = 0;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++) sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
            double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++) v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
        }

        double sum = 0;
        for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++) sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
        double r = sum - 1.0;
        rms += r*r;
        if (fabs(r) > maxr) maxr = fabs(r);
    }

    double frac = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) { double d = fabs(v[i] - floor(v[i]+0.5)); frac += d; }

    ...
}
```

**Phase 1 — pick `n` of `m` equations (strided).**

**Phase 2 — solve the square system.**

|---|---|

So the honest report is: the square solution pins the variables to values that satisfy nothing outside the chosen block. That's expected — the remaining equations are a different overdetermined system, and the variables have no freedom left to meet them.

**Net effect on AIM (48 instances, 100k steps × 20):**

| | init | solved |
|---|---|---|
| full system (current) | 17.2 | 31/48 |
| square subsystem | **16.8** | 31/48 |

/* ---- Gob: linear relaxation of the clause system ------------------------ */

/* Every clause becomes the signed equation sum(+-x) = 1: a positive literal is
 * +x, a negative one -x. Cyclic Kaczmarz projections (one per clause per sweep)
 * solve it in the least-squares sense. Each value is then shifted by the
 * smallest non-negative amount (so -x = 1 decodes to false, not true), rounded,
 * and taken mod 2. A greedy pass then flips a decoded variable whenever it
 * satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks, adapting the bits to the formula.
 * Deterministic, no RNG. */
#define GOB_SWEEPS 64     /* Kaczmarz passes over the whole clause system */
#define GOB_PASSES 4      /* greedy adaptation passes over the decoded bits */

bool solver_init_gob(Solver *s) {
    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);
    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);
    if (!v || !a) { free(v); free(a); return false; }
    for (size_t sweep = 0; sweep < GOB_SWEEPS; sweep++) {
        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++) {
            const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
            size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
            if (len == 0) continue;
            double sum = 0;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
            double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
        }
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        double u = v[i];
        if (u < 0) {                                  /* shift the negative away */
            long long sh = (long long)(-u);
            if ((double)sh < -u) sh++;
            u += (double)sh;
        }
        a[i] = (((long long)(u + 0.5)) & 1) != 0;     /* round to nearest, mod 2 */
    }
    solver_set_assignment(s, a);
    free(v); free(a);
    for (int pass = 0; pass < GOB_PASSES; pass++) {   /* step 4: best correlation */
        size_t flips = 0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
            refresh_var(s, i);
            const VarStats *st = &s->stats[i];
            if (st->make_count > st->break_count) { solver_flip(s, i); flips++; }
        }
        if (flips == 0) break;
    }
    return true;
}

static ResultUnit opt_init(Cli *cli, const char *flag, const char *value) {
    if (strcmp(value, "majority") == 0) cli->cfg.init = INIT_MAJORITY;
    else if (strcmp(value, "rarest") == 0) cli->cfg.init = INIT_RAREST;
    else if (strcmp(value, "glowest") == 0) cli->cfg.init = INIT_GLOWEST;
    else if (strcmp(value, "min-overlapping") == 0) cli->cfg.init = INIT_MIN_OVERLAP;
    else if (strcmp(value, "gob") == 0) cli->cfg.init = INIT_GOB;
    else if (strcmp(value, "likho") == 0) cli->cfg.init = INIT_LIKHO;
    else return ERRF(ResultUnit, ERR_USAGE, "Invalid value for %s: `%s` (expected majority|rarest|glowest|min-overlapping|gob|likho)", flag, value);
    return OK_UNIT(ResultUnit);
}
static ResultUnit opt_pre_cook(Cli *cli, const char *flag, const char *value) {
    if (strcmp(value, "zero") == 0) cli->cfg.likho_pre_cook = INIT_ZERO;
    else if (strcmp(value, "majority") == 0) cli->cfg.likho_pre_cook = INIT_MAJORITY;
    else if (strcmp(value, "rarest") == 0) cli->cfg.likho_pre_cook = INIT_RAREST;
    else if (strcmp(value, "glowest") == 0) cli->cfg.likho_pre_cook = INIT_GLOWEST;
    else if (strcmp(value, "min-overlapping") == 0) cli->cfg.likho_pre_cook = INIT_MIN_OVERLAP;
    else if (strcmp(value, "gob") == 0) cli->cfg.likho_pre_cook = INIT_GOB;
    else return ERRF(ResultUnit, ERR_USAGE, "Invalid value for %s: `%s` (expected zero|majority|rarest|glowest|min-overlapping|gob)", flag, value);
    cli->cfg.init = INIT_LIKHO;   /* pre-cook is a Likho mode */

}

- Variable states (prime/neutral, break/make counts) are derived *lazily*, only for
  the 2-3 variables of the clause actually examined, in one pass. A flip only
  updates clause counters and the rogue-clause index. On random 3-SAT this is
  ~10x faster than re-ranking every variable in every touched clause, with
  identical search decisions (same seed -> same steps).

## Initial assignment (`--init`)

Restart 0 starts from one of six starts (later restarts are always random):

- `--init majority` (default): every variable takes its majority polarity.
- `--init rarest`: deterministic constructive start (no RNG), rarest variables first.
- `--init glowest`: deterministic constructive start, most frequent variables first.
- `--init min-overlapping`: deterministic constructive start, first the most
  frequent variable, then the one overlapping the solved part least.
- `--init gob`: deterministic linear-relaxation start (no RNG), clauses as signed
  equations solved by Kaczmarz sweeps and decoded mod 2.
- `--init likho`: all false, then a neutral/switch-domain repair pass.
- `-deep-dive VARS NODES`: implies `--init likho`, caps switch domains at VARS
  variables, gives each prime at most NODES search nodes, and fires domains
  before neutral repairs.
- `-pre-cook zero|majority|rarest|glowest|min-overlapping|gob`: implies `--init likho`;
  phase 1 is that assignment instead of the default all-false one (a partially
  solved input).

The six starts work in both `plain` and `groups` mode; `-deep-dive` is a variant
of `likho`.

### Rarest / Glowest / Min-overlapping

All three use the same value rule: the picked variable takes the value that
satisfies more **forced** clauses (open clauses where it is the last unset
variable); else more **open** (not yet satisfied) clauses; else the larger total
polarity; else `false`.

They differ only in which unset variable is picked next:

- `rarest` takes the **fewest** clauses holding `x` or `!x`, whichever count is
  larger; `glowest` the **most**. Only clauses that are not yet satisfied count
  (ties by id), recomputed after every assignment, so satisfying a clause removes
  that overlap from every variable still unset.
- `min-overlapping` takes `glowest`'s pick first, then at every step the unset
  variable with the smallest **(occurrences in satisfied clauses) / (total
  occurrences)** (ties by id). A variable that occurs nowhere has no ratio and
  goes last. The point is to keep picking variables mostly outside the clauses
  the first pick already satisfied, instead of following the same subsystem.

### Gob

`--init gob` is a linear relaxation, not a clause walk. Each clause becomes the
signed equation `sum(±x) = 1` (a positive literal is `+x`, a negative one `-x`),
and 64 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps project the all-zero vector onto that system (one
exact projection per clause per sweep). Each value is then shifted by the
smallest non-negative amount, rounded to the nearest integer and taken mod 2,
which decodes the real vector to booleans. The shift is per variable, not global,
because a global shift cannot satisfy mixed-sign units: `(x)` and `(-x)` always
decode to the same parity.

The decode is only a starting point, so four greedy passes follow: a variable
whose bit satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks is flipped, using the same
incremental counts as the search. Deterministic, no RNG.

### Likho

`--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
`false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no

A domain is capped at 8 variables and its closure search at 64 backtracking nodes,
so a prime with an unusually large or conflicting domain is skipped rather than
solved. `-deep-dive VARS NODES` raises or lowers both bounds. With the default
zero start the repair is deterministic for a given formula; `-pre-cook majority`
inherits the majority phase's RNG tie-breaking.

### Measurements

Measured on random 3-SAT, 10 seeds per row (3 seeds for the 5000-var row), 20
restarts, default solver seed. "old" is the previous total-occurrence rarest order,
kept for comparison; "likho-dd" is `-deep-dive 32 128`, "likho-pc" is
`-pre-cook majority`. All nine starts share the same search code:

| instance | broken after init (maj / old / new / glow / mo / gob / likho / dd / pc) | solved | mean flips over solved (maj / old / new / glow / mo / gob / likho / dd / pc) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 vars, ratio 2.0 | 78 / 15 / 28 / 4.5 / 12.7 / 14.2 / 0 / 0.2 / 0 | 10/10 each | 88 / 47 / 67 / 26 / 27 / 110 / 0 / 1 / 0 |
| 1000 vars, ratio 3.5 | 187 / 77 / 98 / 37 / 58 / 61 / 34 / 32 / 10 | 10/10 each | 11.1k / 16.1k / 12.0k / 19.4k / 7.2k / 14.1k / 18.1k / 17.6k / 9.8k |
| 20000 vars, ratio 3.5 | 3802 / 1527 / 2024 / 783 / 1213 / 1275 / 742 / 637 / 209 | 9/10, 9/10, 9/10, 10/10, 8/10, 0/10, 0/10, 0/10, 9/10 | 123k / 169k / 162k / 129k / 143k / — / — / — / 129k |
| 5000 vars, ratio 3.9 | 1098 / 482 / 631 / 274 / 396 / 411 / 385 / 337 / 126 | 2/3 each | 3.06M / 0.76M / 1.84M / 4.40M / 4.40M / 1.88M / 4.40M / 4.40M / 5.68M |
| AIM yes-set, 48 instances | 46 / 18 / 21 / 16.7 / 19.0 / 17.2 / 23 / 22 / 22 | 27 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 31 / 27 | — |

`glowest` is the best init here. It leaves fewer broken clauses than rarest-new on
every random row (4.5 vs 28, 37 vs 98, 274 vs 631, 783 vs 2024) and at 20000/3.5 it
is the only start that solves all 10 seeds (init 783, 129k flips, 0.9 s vs 2.4 s for
majority). On the AIM yes-set it has the lowest init count (16.7) and solves the same
31 instances as rarest. Taking the highest-overlap variables first pays off where
rarest's low-overlap-first pass leaves clauses hanging on a single literal.

`min-overlapping` sits between rarest-new and glowest on init (12.7 / 58 / 396 /
1213 / 19.0 on the same rows) and is the fastest frequency start at 1000/3.5
(7.2k flips vs glowest's 19.4k): after the glowest first pick it keeps choosing
variables mostly outside the solved part, so the search does not re-enter the same
subsystem. It does not scale as well, though: at 20000/3.5 it solves 8/10 where
glowest solves 10/10.

`gob` is competitive at 1000 vars (init 14.2 / 61, next to min-overlapping's
12.7 / 58; 110 / 14.1k flips) and on the AIM yes-set (17.2 broken, second only to
glowest's 16.7, and the same 31/48). At 5000/3.9 its 1.88M mean flips is second
only to rarest-old, but at 20000/3.5 it solves 0/10 like the zero start: 1275
broken clauses still sit in a deep basin. The linear relaxation finds a good
decode, not a good basin.

The zero start still leaves 3-5x fewer broken clauses than majority, and it solves
1000/2.0 outright at init (zero flips), but it is a much deeper local minimum. At
20000/3.5 it solves **0/10** at this budget, where majority and both rarest orders
solve 9/10 (glowest 10/10); fewer broken clauses does not mean an easier search.
`-pre-cook majority` restores the previous majority-start repair exactly (209
broken, 9/10, 129k flips), so pre-cooking is the escape from the zero-start basin.
On the AIM yes-set the zero start matches both rarest orders at 31/48 (majority and
the majority pre-cook stay at 27/48), so the constructive start pays off there.
`-deep-dive 32 128` trims the zero-start init count (637 at 20000, 337 at 5000) but
changes no solved count. From a majority pre-cook, domains-first makes 20000/3.5
much worse (1/10 at 32 128, 0/3 at the default bounds), so deep-dive is not the
escape route; pre-cook without it is. `majority` stays the default start for the
plain search.

The max-of-polarities rarest order leaves 2-3x fewer broken clauses than majority,
but ~30% more than the total-occurrence order. It is faster on 1000-var/3.5 and
20000-var/3.5, slower on 5000-var/3.9; on the AIM yes-set both rarest orders solve
the same 31/48 (identical failure sets) versus 27/48 for majority. It changes which
near-solutions are reachable more than it changes total coverage.

Rarest-first is still **worse** than majority at scale. Why: it satisfies each clause
with the first literal it can and never adds redundancy, so almost
every satisfied clause hangs on a single variable. On the 20000-var / ratio 3.5 instance
77% of variables are prime after rarest-first (62% after majority), only 23% are neutral
(38%), and 63% of the broken clauses contain no neutral variable at all, i.e. no free flip
(26% after majority) -- measured with the old ordering. Fewer problems, but most of the
remaining ones cannot be fixed
without breaking something. Likho attacks exactly that: a prime's switch domain
chains through other primes until it reaches a neutral, instead of giving up at the
first broken clause. Group mode's merge, which only fires neutrals,
is hit the same way: its leftover barely changed (e.g. 105.7 -> 95.0 unmerged at ratio
4.2).

### Coverage: instances no start can solve

The per-start counts above hide whether a failure is shared. Taking the union over
all nine starts:

- **Random 3-SAT: 0 unsolved by all.** Every generated instance in the table was
  solved by at least one start, even where individual starts missed it (e.g. the
  zero-start Likho at 20000/3.5).
- **AIM yes-set: 17 of 48 unsolved by all** (31 covered). Every one is satisfiable,
  so these are budget failures at 100000 steps x 20 restarts, not UNSAT. By size:
  50-var `50-1_6-yes1-{1,2}` (2), 100-var `100-1_6-yes1-{1..4}` and
  `100-2_0-yes1-{1,2,4}` (7), 200-var `200-1_6-yes1-{1..4}` and
  `200-2_0-yes1-{1..4}` (8).
- The AIM union is exactly rarest's 31: `glowest`, `min-overlapping`, `gob`,
  zero-start Likho and deep-dive each solve that identical set, so the extra starts
  add no new instance beyond rarest. Only `majority` and the majority pre-cook miss
  four of them.

Reproduce with `make bench-rarest ARGS="1000 3.5 10 200000 9"` (or
`ARGS="file.cnf 100000 20"`); `steps = 0` measures init quality only. The harness
also reimplements the old total-occurrence order as a baseline, so all nine starts
run the same search code; its glowest row is `--init glowest`, its min-overlapping
row is `--init min-overlapping`, its gob row is `--init gob`, its deep-dive row
uses `-deep-dive 32 128` and its pre-cook row uses `-pre-cook majority`.

Sequential rogue groups with a neutral-driven merge, layered on the same solver

breaks no solved clause (`break_count == 0`), **prime** iff it is the sole
support of at least one (`break_count >= 1`). Neutrality belongs to the *current*

static void test_init_gob_hand_checked(void) {
    /* Units pin the decode: 1 is +x = 1, -2 is -x = 1 (shifted to false), 3 is
     * +x = 1, so the start is exactly (true, false, true). */
    Cnf c = must_parse("p cnf 3 3\n1 0\n-2 0\n3 0\n");
    Solver *s = must_solver(&c, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    const bool *a = solver_assignment(s);
    CHECK(a[0] && !a[1] && a[2]);
    CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&c);

    /* A single clause 1 2 projects to (1/2, 1/2): both round up, so it holds. */
    Cnf d = must_parse("p cnf 2 1\n1 2 0\n");
    s = must_solver(&d, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    a = solver_assignment(s);
    CHECK(a[0] && a[1] && solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&d);

    /* Mixed signs: (1 -2) projects to (1/2, -1/2); -1/2 shifts to +1/2, so both
     * decode true and the clause holds. */
    Cnf e = must_parse("p cnf 2 1\n1 -2 0\n");
    s = must_solver(&e, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    a = solver_assignment(s);
    CHECK(a[0] && a[1] && solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&e);

    /* Empty clause and empty formula: no crash, the empty clause stays rogue. */
    Cnf f = must_parse("p cnf 1 1\n0\n");
    s = must_solver(&f, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 1);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&f);

    Cnf g = must_parse("p cnf 0 0\n");
    s = must_solver(&g, 1);
    CHECK(solver_init_gob(s));
    CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(s) == 0);
    solver_free(s); cnf_free(&g);
}

static void test_init_gob_properties(void) {
    SolverConfig cfg = solver_config_default();
    cfg.init = INIT_GOB;
    cfg.max_steps = 20000; cfg.restarts = 2;
    for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
        int n = 60 + 20 * (i % 4);
        Cnf c = random_cnf(n, (int)(n * (2.0 + 0.4 * (i % 5))), 900 + (uint64_t)i);
        Solver *a = must_solver(&c, 1), *b = must_solver(&c, 99);   /* different RNG seeds: no randomness used */
        CHECK(solver_init_gob(a) && solver_init_gob(b));
        CHECK(memcmp(solver_assignment(a), solver_assignment(b), c.n_vars) == 0);   /* deterministic */
        CHECK(solver_unsatisfied_count(a) == brute_unsat(&c, solver_assignment(a))); /* counters consistent */
        solver_free(a); solver_free(b);

        Solver *s = must_solver(&c, 5);                       /* plain solver from the gob start */
        ResultSolve r = solver_solve(s, &cfg);
        CHECK(r.ok);
        if (r.ok && r.val.status == SOLVE_SAT) CHECK(verify(&c, r.val.assignment, r.val.n_vars));
        if (r.ok) solve_result_free(&r.val);
        solver_free(s);

        GroupConfig gc = group_config_default();               /* and the group solver */
        gc.max_groups = 64;
        ResultGroup g = group_solve(&c, &cfg, &gc);
        CHECK(g.ok);
        if (g.ok) { check_group_result(&c, &g.val); group_result_free(&g.val); }
        cnf_free(&c);
    }
}

static ResultInt solve_and_report(const Cnf *cnf, const Cli *cli) {
    if (!cnf_is_3sat(cnf))
        fprintf(stderr, "Warning: input contains clauses longer than 3 literals; solving general CNF instead of strict 3-SAT.\n");
    if (cli->groups_mode) return solve_groups_and_report(cnf, cli);
    Solver *solver = TRY(ResultInt, solver_new(cnf, cli->cfg.seed));
    ResultSolve rs = solver_solve(solver, &cli->cfg);
    solver_free(solver);
    SolveResult res = TRY(ResultInt, rs);

    if (res.status == SOLVE_SAT && !verify(cnf, res.assignment, res.n_vars)) {
        solve_result_free(&res);
        return ERRF(ResultInt, ERR_VERIFY, "Internal verification failed");
    }
    ResultUnit w = write_json(cli->output, cnf, &res);
    if (!w.ok) { solve_result_free(&res); return ERR(ResultInt, w.err); }

    int code;
    if (res.status == SOLVE_SAT) {
        printf("SAT (%zu steps, restart %zu) \xe2\x80\x94 %s\n", res.steps, res.restart, cli->output);
        code = 0;
    } else if (res.status == SOLVE_UNSAT) {
        printf("UNSAT (%zu contradiction%s) \xe2\x80\x94 %s\n",
               res.n_contradictions, res.n_contradictions == 1 ? "" : "s", cli->output);
        for (size_t i = 0; i < res.n_contradictions; i++)
            printf("  clause %zu == not clause %zu\n", res.contradictions[i].b, res.contradictions[i].a);
        code = 4;
    } else {
        printf("UNKNOWN (%zu steps, best %zu unsatisfied) \xe2\x80\x94 %s\n", res.steps, res.best_unsatisfied, cli->output);
        code = 3;
    }
    solve_result_free(&res);
    return OK(ResultInt, code);
}

static ResultInt run(int argc, char **argv) {
    Cli cli = { .input = NULL, .output = DEFAULT_OUT, .cfg = solver_config_default(),
                .groups_mode = false, .gcfg = group_config_default() };
    TRY0(ResultInt, parse_args(argc, argv, &cli));
    Cnf cnf = TRY_CTX(ResultInt, cnf_from_dimacs_file(cli.input), "Failed to load CNF");
    ResultInt r = solve_and_report(&cnf, &cli);
    cnf_free(&cnf);
    return r;
}

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    ResultInt r = run(argc, argv);
    if (r.ok) return r.val;
    fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", r.err.msg);
    if (r.err.kind == ERR_USAGE) { usage(); return 2; }
    return 1;
}

```c
/* Shift each real value to the nearest non-negative integer, take it mod 2, and
 * repair the decoded bits with GOB_PASSES greedy flips. Shared by both gob starts. */
static void gob_decode_and_repair(Solver *s, const double *v, bool *a) {
    size_t nv = s->cnf->n_vars;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        double u = v[i];
        if (u < 0) {
            long long sh = (long long)(-u);
            if ((double)sh < -u) sh++;
            u += (double)sh;
        }
        a[i] = (((long long)(u + 0.5)) & 1) != 0;
    }
    solver_set_assignment(s, a);
    for (int pass = 0; pass < GOB_PASSES; pass++) {
        size_t flips = 0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
            refresh_var(s, i);
            const VarStats *st = &s->stats[i];
            if (st->make_count > st->break_count) { solver_flip(s, i); flips++; }
        }
        if (flips == 0) break;
    }
}
```

```c
static void gob_project(const Cnf *cnf, double *v, size_t ci) {
    const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
    size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
    if (len == 0) return;
    double sum = 0;
    for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
        sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
    double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
    for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
        v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
}
```

```c
bool solver_init_gob_square(Solver *s, GobSquareCheck *check) {
    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);
    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);
    bool *sel = calloc(nc ? nc : 1, 1);
    if (!v || !a || !sel) { free(v); free(a); free(sel); return false; }
    size_t neq = nv < nc ? nv : nc;                 /* phase 1: n of m, strided */
    for (size_t ei = 0; ei < neq; ei++) sel[ei * nc / neq] = true;
    for (size_t sweep = 0; sweep < GOB_SQUARE_SWEEPS; sweep++)   /* phase 2 */
        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++)
            if (sel[ci]) gob_project(cnf, v, ci);
    if (check) {                                    /* phase 3: the rest of the system */
        check->selected_bad = check->other_bad = check->other_total = 0;
        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++) {
            const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
            size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
            double sum = 0;
            for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
                sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
            bool bad = len && (sum < 1.0 - 1e-9 || sum > 1.0 + 1e-9);
            if (sel[ci]) { if (bad) check->selected_bad++; }
            else { check->other_total++; if (bad) check->other_bad++; }
        }
    }
    gob_decode_and_repair(s, v, a);
    free(v); free(a); free(sel);
    return true;
}
```

  goes last. The point is to keep picking variables mostly outside the clauses
  the first pick already satisfied, instead of following the same subsystem.

### Gob

`--init gob` is a linear relaxation, not a clause walk. Each clause becomes the
signed equation `sum(±x) = 1` (a positive literal is `+x`, a negative one `-x`),
and 64 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps project the all-zero vector onto that system (one
exact projection per clause per sweep). Each value is then shifted by the
smallest non-negative amount, rounded to the nearest integer and taken mod 2,
which decodes the real vector to booleans. The shift is per variable, not global,
because a global shift cannot satisfy mixed-sign units: `(x)` and `(-x)` always
decode to the same parity.

The decode is only a starting point, so four greedy passes follow: a variable
whose bit satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks is flipped, using the same
incremental counts as the search. Deterministic, no RNG.

### Gob-square

`--init gob-square` runs the same idea in three phases:

1. **Pick a square subsystem.** Of the `m` equations, select `n` (one every
   `m/n` clauses), so the selected block has as many equations as variables.
2. **Solve it.** 512 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps over the selected rows only (the
   square system converges slower than the full one, hence the larger sweep
   count).
3. **Check the rest.** Every unselected equation is evaluated on that solution.
   `GobSquareCheck` reports `selected_bad`, `other_bad` and `other_total`; the
   bench harness prints the averages as `gob-square phase 3`.

The solution is then decoded and repaired exactly like `gob`. This is still a
seed, not a solve: the selected rows can be linearly dependent (strided
selection makes no rank guarantee, e.g. `aim-50-3_4-yes1-1` is singular at
49/50), the values are fractional, and on the AIM corpus phase 3 finds almost
every unselected equation violated (`rest_bad` 30/30, 99/100, 200/200 on the
50-, 100- and 200-var rows checked). Reporting "no solution" is the expected
answer for `m > n`; the decode is what the search gets.

### Likho

`--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
`false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no
satisfied clause, and each variable is flipped at most once:

- A **neutral** variable inside a rogue clause is flipped immediately; it breaks
  nothing and satisfies at least that clause.
- A **prime** is the sole support of some satisfied clause, so flipping it alone
  breaks that clause. Its **switch domain** is the set of other unflipped variables

bool solver_init_min_overlap(Solver *s) { return init_order(s, ORDER_MIN_OVERLAP); }

/* ---- Gob: linear relaxation of the clause system ------------------------ */

/* Every clause becomes the signed equation sum(+-x) = 1: a positive literal is
 * +x, a negative one -x. Cyclic Kaczmarz projections (one per clause per sweep)
 * solve it in the least-squares sense. Each value is then shifted by the
 * smallest non-negative amount (so -x = 1 decodes to false, not true), rounded,
 * and taken mod 2. A greedy pass then flips a decoded variable whenever it
 * satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks, adapting the bits to the formula.
 * Deterministic, no RNG. */
#define GOB_SWEEPS 64     /* Kaczmarz passes over the whole clause system */
#define GOB_SQUARE_SWEEPS 512  /* the square system converges slower than the full one */
#define GOB_PASSES 4      /* greedy adaptation passes over the decoded bits */

/* One exact Kaczmarz projection of the real vector onto clause ci's equation. */
static void gob_project(const Cnf *cnf, double *v, size_t ci) {
    const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
    size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
    if (len == 0) return;
    double sum = 0;
    for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
        sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
    double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
    for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
        v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
}

/* Decode the real vector to booleans, then run the greedy repair passes. */
static void gob_decode_and_repair(Solver *s, const double *v, bool *a) {
    size_t nv = s->cnf->n_vars;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        double u = v[i];
        if (u < 0) {                                  /* shift the negative away */
            long long sh = (long long)(-u);
            if ((double)sh < -u) sh++;
            u += (double)sh;
        }
        a[i] = (((long long)(u + 0.5)) & 1) != 0;     /* round to nearest, mod 2 */
    }
    solver_set_assignment(s, a);
    for (int pass = 0; pass < GOB_PASSES; pass++) {   /* step 4: best correlation */
        size_t flips = 0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
            refresh_var(s, i);
            const VarStats *st = &s->stats[i];
            if (st->make_count > st->break_count) { solver_flip(s, i); flips++; }
        }
        if (flips == 0) break;
    }
}

bool solver_init_gob(Solver *s) {
    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);
    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);
    if (!v || !a) { free(v); free(a); return false; }
    for (size_t sweep = 0; sweep < GOB_SWEEPS; sweep++)
        for (size_t ci = 0; ci < nc; ci++) gob_project(cnf, v, ci);
    gob_decode_and_repair(s, v, a);
    free(v); free(a);
    return true;
}

bool solver_init_gob_square(Solver *s, GobSquareCheck *check) {
    const Cnf *cnf = s->cnf;
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    double *v = calloc(nv ? nv : 1, sizeof *v);
    bool *a = malloc((nv ? nv : 1) * sizeof *a);

### Gob-square

`--init gob-square` runs the same idea in three phases:

1. **Pick a square subsystem.** Of the `m` equations, select `n` (one every
   `m/n` clauses), so the selected block has as many equations as variables.
2. **Solve it.** 512 cyclic Kaczmarz sweeps over the selected rows only (the
   square system converges slower than the full one, hence the larger sweep
   count).
3. **Check the rest.** Every unselected equation is evaluated on that solution.
   `GobSquareCheck` reports `selected_bad`, `other_bad` and `other_total`; the
   bench harness prints the averages as `gob-square phase 3`.

The solution is then decoded and repaired exactly like `gob`. This is still a
seed, not a solve: the selected rows can be linearly dependent (strided
selection makes no rank guarantee, e.g. `aim-50-3_4-yes1-1` is singular at
49/50), the values are fractional, and on the AIM corpus phase 3 finds almost
every unselected equation violated (`rest_bad` 30/30, 99/100, 200/200 on the
50-, 100- and 200-var rows checked). Reporting "no solution" is the expected
answer for `m > n`; the decode is what the search gets.

### Likho

`--init likho` starts from `-pre-cook` (`zero`, the default: every variable
`false`), then repairs rogue clauses. It only accepts moves that break no
satisfied clause, and each variable is flipped at most once:
=== 229,242
zero start: 1275 broken clauses still sit in a deep basin. The linear relaxation
finds a good decode, not a good basin.

`gob-square` shows what the square subsystem does and does not buy. Its phase-3
report says the solution does not satisfy the system: at 1000 vars ~89% of the
selected rows and every unselected row are violated, and at 20000 vars
17.8k of 20000 selected and 50.0k of 50.0k unselected. Kaczmarz has not converged
in 512 sweeps, and with `m > n` the full system has no exact solution anyway.
As a seed it is the second-best init on the AIM yes-set (16.8, behind glowest's
16.7) and solves the same 31/48, but on random 3-SAT it is worse than the
full-system gob on every row (19.2 vs 14.2, 71.5 vs 60.6, 1380 vs 1275, 436 vs
411 broken) and changes no solved count, for 8x the sweeps.

The zero start still leaves 3-5x fewer broken clauses than majority, and it solves

```c
#include "sat.h"
#include <math.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef struct { uint64_t s; } R;
static uint64_t nx(R *r) { uint64_t x = r->s; x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17; return r->s = x; }
static size_t idx(R *r, size_t n) { return (size_t)(nx(r) % n); }

typedef struct { size_t nv, nc, *off; int *lits; } Gen;

static Gen gen3(size_t nv, size_t nc, uint64_t seed) {
    Gen g = { nv, nc, malloc((nc + 1) * sizeof *g.off), malloc(nc * 3 * sizeof *g.lits) };
    R r = { seed ? seed : 1 };
    g.off[0] = 0;
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++) {
        size_t a = idx(&r, nv), b = idx(&r, nv - 1), d = idx(&r, nv - 2);
        if (b >= a) b++;
        if (d >= a) d++;
        if (d >= b) d++;
        g.lits[c*3+0] = ((int)a + 1) * (nx(&r) & 1 ? 1 : -1);
        g.lits[c*3+1] = ((int)b + 1) * (nx(&r) & 1 ? 1 : -1);
        g.lits[c*3+2] = ((int)d + 1) * (nx(&r) & 1 ? 1 : -1);
        g.off[c+1] = g.off[c] + 3;
    }
    return g;
}
```

static void gen_free(Gen *g) { free(g->off); free(g->lits); }

/* Three distinct variables per clause, random polarity. */
static Gen gen3(size_t nv, size_t nc, uint64_t seed) {
    Gen g = { nv, nc, malloc((nc + 1) * sizeof *g.off), malloc(nc * 3 * sizeof *g.lits) };
    R r = { seed ? seed : 1 };
    g.off[0] = 0;
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++) {
        size_t a = idx(&r, nv), b = idx(&r, nv - 1), d = idx(&r, nv - 2);
        if (b >= a) b++;
        if (d >= a) d++;
        if (d >= b) d++;
        int s[3];
        for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) s[k] = (nx(&r) & 1) ? 1 : -1;
        g.lits[3*c+0] = s[0] * (int)(a + 1);
        g.lits[3*c+1] = s[1] * (int)(b + 1);
        g.lits[3*c+2] = s[2] * (int)(d + 1);
        g.off[c+1] = g.off[c] + 3;
    }
    return g;
}

static char *to_dimacs(const Gen *g) {
    size_t cap = g->nc * 32 + 64;
    char *s = malloc(cap), *p = s;
    p += sprintf(p, "p cnf %zu %zu\n", g->nv, g->nc);
    for (size_t c = 0; c < g->nc; c++) {
        for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) p += sprintf(p, "%d ", g->lits[3*c+k]);
        *p++ = '0'; *p++ = '\n'; *p = '\0';
    }
    return s;
}

/* ---- old rarest: static order by total occurrences, ties by id --------- */

static void old_rarest(const Cnf *cnf, bool *a) {
    size_t nv = cnf->n_vars, nc = cnf->n_clauses;
    size_t *cnt = calloc(nv, sizeof *cnt), *order = malloc(nv * sizeof *order);
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++)
        for (size_t k = 0; k < cnf_clause_len(cnf, c); k++) cnt[cnf_clause(cnf, c)[k].var]++;
    for (size_t v = 0; v < nv; v++) order[v] = v;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++)
        for (size_t j = i + 1; j < nv; j++)
            if (cnt[order[j]] < cnt[order[i]]) { size_t t = order[i]; order[i] = order[j]; order[j] = t; }
    uint32_t *unset = malloc(nc * sizeof *unset);
    unsigned char *done = calloc(nc, 1);
    for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++) unset[c] = (uint32_t)cnf_clause_len(cnf, c);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
        size_t v = order[i], fp = 0, fn = 0, op = 0, on = 0, tp = 0, tn = 0;
        for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++)
            for (size_t k = 0; k < cnf_clause_len(cnf, c); k++) {
                const Lit l = cnf_clause(cnf, c)[k];
                if (l.var != v) continue;
                if (l.positive) tp++; else tn++;
                if (done[c]) continue;
                if (unset[c] == 1) { if (l.positive) fp++; else fn++; }
                else { if (l.positive) op++; else on++; }
            }
        bool val = (fp != fn) ? fp > fn : (op != on) ? op > on : (tp != tn) ? tp > tn : false;
        a[v] = val;
        for (size_t c = 0; c < nc; c++)
            for (size_t k = 0; k < cnf_clause_len(cnf, c); k++) {
                const Lit l = cnf_clause(cnf, c)[k];
                if (l.var != v) continue;
                unset[c]--;
                if (!done[c] && l.positive == val) done[c] = 1;
            }
    }
    free(cnt); free(order); free(unset); free(done);
}

i < cnf.n_vars; i++) {\n            if (adec[i] == astar[i]) agr_dec++;\n            if (agob[i] == astar[i]) agr_gob++;\n            double x = astar[i] ? 1.0 : -1.0;\n            dot += x * v[i];\n            nv2 += v[i] * v[i];\n        }\n        double corr = nv2 > 0 ? dot / (sqrt((double)cnf.n_vars) * sqrt(nv2)) : 0;\n\n        /* Project astar itself onto the system: how far does it have to move? */\n        double *w = malloc(cnf.n_vars * sizeof *w);\n        for (size_t i = 0; While that reruns, I pinned down the earlier seed-5 mismatch: it's a **pre-existing bug in `tools/bench_rarest.c`'s generator**, not in the analysis.

`gen3` tries to keep the three variables distinct with

```c
if (b >= a) b++;
if (d >= a) d++;
if (d >= b) d++;
```

which fails when `b < a`: e.g. `a=5, b=3, d=4` → `d` becomes `5`, i.e. the same variable twice. The parser then drops the tautologies and shortens the same-sign duplicates to 2-literal clauses. Measured on the 20000/3.5 row: **17 repeated-variable clauses out of ~700k (0.0024%)**, ~1.7 per instance.

Second effect: the harness feeds the *parsed* clause count into the next seed (`nv = cnf.n_vars; nc = cnf.n_clauses;`), so the corpus drifts 70000 → 69990 over the 10 seeds. That is why my first tool generated different instances than the bench and seed 5 disagreed. The tool now replicates the drift, so the set matches the bench exactly.

Both are harness quirks, not solver bugs; the README numbers stay internally consistent (every start sees the same instance). Fixing `gen3` would shift every published number, so I have not touched it.

## Result

**The qualifying set is 10 instances, all from the 20000/3.5 row.** On AIM, `glowest` and `gob` solve the *same* 31/48, so `glowest`-solved − `gob`-solved is empty. On 5000/3.9 the two agree on every seed (both solve seed 1, both fail 2–3). Only 20000/3.5 splits: glowest 10/10, gob 0/10.

### 1. The equation is the wrong target

`sum(±x) = 1` over a 3-literal clause means **exactly two literals true**. Counted on glowest's actual satisfying assignment (`a*`), across 70 000 clauses:

| clause sum | literals true | count |
|---|---|---|
| +1 | 2 | ~29 400 (42%) |
| +3 | 3 | ~10 300 (15%) |
| −1 | **1** | **~30 300 (43%)** |
| −3 | 0 | 0 |

So 58% of a satisfying assignment's clauses violate their equation, mostly by 2. Predicted RMS = √(4·0.58) = 1.52 — exactly the measured `rmsA*` = **1.52**. Kaczmarz's own vector sits at **1.19**, i.e. *closer to the linear system than a real solution is*. The residual minimum is not near SAT; it is past it.

### 2. The correlation is real but weak

Against `a*`, per instance: Pearson **0.32** (mean-centred identical), sign agreement **63.5%**, chance is 50% ± 0.35% at n=20 000 — so not noise, but ~7 300 variables disagree. The existing decode (shift negatives up, round, mod 2) keeps only **52.5%**, and gob's greedy repair lifts that to **60%**.

### 3. The decode, not the system, is losing the signal

I ran the same `v` through two decodes and local search (200k steps × 10, same budget gob fails with):

| start | unsat clauses at init | solved |
|---|---|---|
| glowest's own start | ~812 | 10/10 |
| gob (decode + greedy) | 1 270 | 0/10 |
| sign(v) | 5 380 | **6/10** |
| shift/round/mod-2 decode | 8 256 | 0/10 |
| random | ~46 900 | — |

Sign decoding solves 6/10 where gob's decode solves 0/10. So the linear system **does** carry usable signal; `ceil(-v)`/round/parity inverts it. For `v ∈ (−0.5, 0)` the shift makes the bit `1`, flipping the sign, and values past ±1.5 wrap under mod 2 — together they destroy most of the 63.5% agreement.

Also worth noting: greedy repair cuts unsat 8 256 → 1 270 (near glowest's 812) yet solves nothing, while the un-repaired sign start at 5 380 solves 6/10. Clause-count hill-climbing is landing in a worse basin.

### Conclusion
The linear system is a genuine but weaker signal than glowest's overlap start. Gob's failure is explained twice over: the equation asks for "exactly 2 true", which most satisfying clauses don't satisfy, and the parity decode then throws away the sign agreement that survives. `gob-square` shares that decode, so it inherits the same loss.

Skipped: I changed nothing in the repo. Switching the decode to sign would be a one-line-ish experiment but shifts every published gob/gob-square number, so I left it for you to call. Risk: `a*` is one of many solutions, so 63.5% may understate the true correlation — a nearest-solution measure could be higher, but the init-unsat and 6/10 results don't depend on that choice.

739: /* ---- Gob: linear relaxation of the clause system (full or square) ------ */
740: 
741: /* Every clause becomes the signed equation sum(+-x) = 1: a positive literal is
742:  * +x, a negative one -x. Cyclic Kaczmarz projections (one per clause per sweep)
743:  * solve it in the least-squares sense. Each value is then shifted by the
744:  * smallest non-negative amount (so -x = 1 decodes to false, not true), rounded,
745:  * and taken mod 2. A greedy pass then flips a decoded variable whenever it
746:  * satisfies more rogue clauses than it breaks, adapting the bits to the formula.
747:  * Deterministic, no RNG. */
748: #define GOB_SWEEPS 64     /* Kaczmarz passes over the whole clause system */
749: #define GOB_SQUARE_SWEEPS 512  /* the square system converges slower than the full one */
750: #define GOB_PASSES 4      /* greedy adaptation passes over the decoded bits */
751: 
752: /* One exact Kaczmarz projection of the real vector onto clause ci's equation. */
753: static void gob_project(const Cnf *cnf, double *v, size_t ci) {
754:     const Lit *cl = cnf_clause(cnf, ci);
755:     size_t len = cnf_clause_len(cnf, ci);
756:     if (len == 0) return;
757:     double sum = 0;
758:     for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
759:         sum += cl[k].positive ? v[cl[k].var] : -v[cl[k].var];
760:     double step = (1.0 - sum) / (double)len;
761:     for (size_t k = 0; k < len; k++)
762:         v[cl[k].var] += cl[k].positive ? step : -step;
763: }
764: 
765: /* Decode the real vector to booleans, then run the greedy repair passes. */
766: static void gob_decode_and_repair(Solver *s, const double *v, bool *a) {
767:     size_t nv = s->cnf->n_vars;
768:     for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
769:         double u = v[i];
770:         if (u < 0) {                                  /* shift the negative away */
771:             long long sh = (long long)(-u);
772:             if ((double)sh < -u) sh++;
773:             u += (double)sh;
774:         }
775:         a[i] = (((long long)(u + 0.5)) & 1) != 0;     /* round to nearest, mod 2 */
776:     }
777:     solver_set_assignment(s, a);
778:     for (int pass = 0; pass < GOB_PASSES; pass++) {   /* step 4: best correlation */
779:         size_t flips = 0;
780:         for (size_t i = 0; i < nv; i++) {
781:             refresh_var(s, i);
782:             const VarStats *st = &s->stats[i];
783:             if (st->make_count > st->break_count) { solver_flip(s, i); flips++; }
784:         }
785:         if (flips == 0) break;
786:     }
787: }
